      feedback: National, nationalise and nationalisation are formed from it.
    - id: b
      text: It remains Latin.
      feedback: It is integrated into English.
    - id: c
      text: It cannot take affixes.
      feedback: It does.
  - answer: a

### Section: Chapter Review
Three questions organise everything in this chapter. Is the form grammatical? Is it established? And if it is both, what internal structure does it have? *Kingdom* is established, *policeability* is grammatical without being established, and a nonce-word is the second kind, used once and dropped. None of those verdicts is about taste.

Complex words are bases and affixes arranged in layers, and the arrangement explains behaviour that a flat list of pieces cannot. Productivity and lexicalisation account for the gap between a pattern that still makes words and a formation surviving only in what it has already made. Around the edges sit manufacture, initialism, clipping, blending, back-formation and phonological modification.

Conversion shifts a word between categories without changing its form. Compounding joins bases into nouns, adjectives and verbs, classical combining forms included. Derivation supplies negation, evaluation, gender, location, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation and the numeral patterns — most of the vocabulary-building machinery English has.

#### A word-formation checklist
Identify the base and the process: conversion, compounding, derivation, clipping, blending or back-formation. Check whether the pattern is productive and whether the result is established, potential or nonce. Then analyse the constituent structure and the meaning relation between the parts.

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes established and potential words?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: Established words are familiar vocabulary items; potential words are grammatical but not established.
      feedback: Policeability is potential; kingdom is established.
    - id: b
      text: Potential words are always ungrammatical.
      feedback: They are grammatical.
    - id: c
      text: Established words are always morphologically simple.
      feedback: Many are complex.
  - answer: a

## Teaching blocks
### Teaching block 1
Say *ungentlemanly* slowly and you can feel the seams: a negative prefix outside, an adjective-making suffix within, a compound underneath that. English keeps building words this way, and speakers keep accepting some of the results while letting others pass. Lexical word-formation is the study of that construction — the shaping of new bases and new lexemes — where inflection only reshapes words that already exist.

### Teaching block 2
The account opens with the gap between a word a dictionary lists and a word the grammar merely permits, then examines the internal anatomy of complex words and the reasons why one pattern keeps minting new items while another survives only in what it has already made. From there it works through the minor processes — clipping, blending, back-formation, conversion — before settling into compounding and the affixation patterns that do most of the labour: negation, evaluation, gender, place, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation, numerals.

### Teaching block 3
Two questions run underneath everything. Is the form grammatical, and is it established? They have different answers and different kinds of evidence, and holding them apart is most of the analytical discipline the chapter asks for.

### Teaching block 4
*Kingdom* and *bishopric* sit in the dictionary, and so do *unfaithfulness* and *infidelity*, even though those two look nothing alike inside. These are established words: items a speaker knows individually and a dictionary lists. The match is imperfect: dictionaries also carry multiword expressions whose meaning is idiomatic, so dictionary entries and morphological words are not the same inventory.

### Teaching block 5
Now try *policeability*. Nothing in it is strange — *police* takes *-able*, and *-able* takes a nominalising suffix — yet it will not be in the dictionary. That is a potential word: morphologically well formed, not established. *Priestric* and *pick-basket* fail differently. The *-ric* of *bishopric* no longer forms new words, and the verb-plus-object pattern behind *pick-basket* is closed as well, so these strings are not merely unused but unavailable.

### Teaching block 6
A nonce-word goes one step further into use: coined on a particular occasion, understood in context, never adopted. Every nonce-word is a potential word, but most potential words have never been uttered at all. And disliking a well-formed coinage settles nothing about its grammar. That is a judgement of taste, not of morphology.

### Teaching block 7
Word status

### Teaching block 8
Established | kingdom | Familiar vocabulary item

### Teaching block 9
Potential | policeability | Well formed but not established

### Teaching block 10
Nonce | a one-off coinage | Used but not established

### Teaching block 11
Ungrammatical | priestric | Does not conform to current rules

### Teaching block 12
Multiword dictionary item | give in | Listed but not a morphological word

### Teaching block 13
*Mouse-trap*, *child-care* and *elephant-tusk* come apart into two bases each; *entrap*, *childish* and *elephantine* come apart into a base plus an affix. That is the first cut to make. A complex word can be analysed into smaller units, a simple word cannot, and the units doing the central work are bases — with affixes as the bound elements that attach to them.

### Teaching block 14
Most English bases stand alone, which is exactly why the bound ones are easy to miss. *Dur-* in *durable*, *aggress-* in *aggressive*, the bases of *pre-empt* and *disperse*. None stands alone, yet each fills the base slot and takes the affixes a base takes. Their Latin and French provenance explains the oddity: they arrived already attached.

### Teaching block 15
Classical combining forms are the strangest members of the family: *anglo-*, *aster-*, *auto-*, *electro-*, *pseudo-*. They are bound, so they cannot stand alone, and they lean towards affix-like behaviour. But they pair with other combining forms, as in *electrolysis*, or with free bases, as in *electromagnet*, and they bring lexical meaning of their own rather than grammatical modification.

### Teaching block 16
Morphological units

### Teaching block 17
Free base | trap, child | Can stand alone

### Teaching block 18
Bound base | dur-, aggress- | Cannot stand alone

### Teaching block 19
Combining form | electro-, pseudo- | Classical bound base

### Teaching block 20
Prefix | en-, un-, pre- | Before the base

### Teaching block 21
Suffix | -ish, -ly, -able | After the base

### Teaching block 22
Where does the first cut fall in *ungentlemanly*? Not between *ungentleman* and *ly*, since there is no such base, but between *un* and *gentlemanly*. *Gentlemanly* divides again into *gentleman* + *ly*, and *gentleman* into *gentle* + *man*. Only one ordering matches how the word is built, and only that ordering predicts which pieces behave alike.

### Teaching block 23
That ordering is the word’s constituent structure, and it tells you what sort of base each layer is. *Gentleman* is a compound base, because its immediate constituents are bases; *gentlemanly* is a derivative base, because one immediate constituent is an affix; *gentle* and *man* are simple. A lexical base, finally, is not contained in any larger base formed by word-formation.

### Teaching block 24
The same string changes job with its surroundings. *Gentleman* is a word in *He behaves like a gentleman*, but inside *gentlemanly* it is only a base; *gentle* and *man* are bases within *gentleman* and are not words there. Wordhood belongs to a use, not to a permanent label attached to a sequence of letters.

### Teaching block 25
un + gentlemanly — The first division is prefix plus derivative base.

### Teaching block 26
gentleman + ly — Gentlemanly is a derivative base.

### Teaching block 27
gentle + man — Gentleman is a compound base.

### Teaching block 28
dis + interested + ness — Layered derivation with a compound-like base.

### Teaching block 29
Why does *policeability* feel available while *priestric* feels shut? Both are assembled from real pieces. The difference is productivity: *-able* and *-ness* still recruit new bases, whereas *-ric* survives only in formations already made. Availability, not shape, is what a productive pattern offers.

### Teaching block 30
Establishment can also bury a formation’s parts. Anyone can parse *blackmail* into *black* and *mail*, and nobody predicts its sense from them. *Blackguard* has travelled further still: the compound is no longer recoverable, so the word is now a simple base. Lexicalisation names that drift — a formation settling into a lexical item with a meaning and history of its own.

### Teaching block 31
Patterns run from wide open through semi-productive to a closed list of survivors; productivity is not a switch. Blocking can keep a well-formed newcomer out when an established synonym already covers the ground. Frequency, register and fashion sort the remainder.

### Teaching block 32
police + able + ity — Potential word formed by productive suffixes.

### Teaching block 33
bishop + ric — Established word with a non-productive suffix.

### Teaching block 34
blackmail — Morphologically analysable but semantically opaque.

### Teaching block 35
blackguard — Historically compound, now a simple base.

### Teaching block 36
Some new words arrive without any morphology worth the name. *Kodak* was invented outright; *Xerox* began as a brand. Initialisms press the opening letters of a phrase into service, whether read letter by letter, as in *BBC*, or as a word, as in *NATO* and *aids*. Clipping simply cuts: *advertisement* to *ad*, *gymnasium* to *gym*, *influenza* to *flu*.

### Teaching block 37
Clipping can also dress up what it leaves. *Comfortable* becomes *comfy*, *television* becomes *telly*, a suffix or a fresh ending doing the cosmetic work. Blending welds two words at the seam — *smoke* and *fog* give *smog*, *breakfast* and *lunch* give *brunch* — while back-formation runs derivation backwards and strips an affix that was never really an affix: *editor* yields *edit*, *burglar* yields *burgle*.

### Teaching block 38
A smaller set works on sound rather than structure. *Teeny* trims and raises *tiny*; *flip-flop* and *ping-pong* echo themselves. These sit at the margin of derivation and compounding, and yet each is productive in its own narrow domain.

### Teaching block 39
Minor processes

### Teaching block 40
Manufacture | Kodak | Invented brand name

### Teaching block 41
Initialism | BBC | Initial letters

### Teaching block 42
Clipping | ad | Shortened word

### Teaching block 43
Embellished clipping | comfy | Clipping plus ending

### Teaching block 44
Blending | smog | Parts of two words

### Teaching block 45
Back-formation | edit | Remove an affix

### Teaching block 46
Phonological modification | teeny | Sound change

### Teaching block 47
Nothing is added and nothing removed. *Google* becomes *to google*, *email* becomes *to email*, *empty* becomes *to empty*: the written form holds still while the category and the meaning move. Conversion, as the name says, moves a word from one class to another with no affix to show for it.

### Teaching block 48
Direction shapes the sense. Nouns turning into verbs usually gain an activity or instrument reading — *to bottle*, *to shelve*, *to network* — and verbs turning into nouns often name an instance or a result: *a run*, *a build*, *a reply*. Adjective-to-noun conversion can be fully institutionalised, as with *the poor*, or flicker in and out of context, as with *the rich*.

### Teaching block 49
Pronunciation sometimes carries a contrast that spelling hides. The noun *permit* and the verb *permit* look identical on the page, and *record* behaves the same way; in speech the stress differs, and with the stress goes the grammar. The change is lexical and syntactic, not inflectional; no paradigm is involved.

### Teaching block 50
Google → to google — Noun to verb.

### Teaching block 51
bottle → to bottle — Noun to verb.

### Teaching block 52
run → a run — Verb to noun.

### Teaching block 53
empty → to empty — Adjective to verb.

### Teaching block 54
Two bases can fuse into a single lexical unit whose meaning is narrower than its parts suggest. *Bedroom*, *blackbird*, *language teacher*, *passer-by*: a *blackbird* names a species, not any bird that happens to be black. The compound names a category, which is not the same as describing a scene.

### Teaching block 55
Most compound nouns are built around a noun head — *bedroom*, *mouse-trap*, *child-care* — but verbs get in as well. *Pickpocket*, *breakwater* and *drawbridge* each contain one, and *pickpocket* names a person rather than a thing, which is the compound’s own doing rather than anything the head predicts. The head still fixes the category and usually the core meaning.

### Teaching block 56
Spelling will not settle compound status. The same formation may be written solid, hyphenated or open, and the choice shifts with fashion. Stress and meaning are better guides. *A blackbird* takes its main stress on the first element; *a black bird* takes it on the adjective: one is a word, the other a phrase.

### Teaching block 57
bedroom — Noun-centred compound.

### Teaching block 58
mouse-trap — Noun-centred compound with a trap head.

### Teaching block 59
pickpocket — Verb-object compound naming a person.

### Teaching block 60
passer-by — Compound with a verb-derived head.

### Teaching block 61
In *well-known*, *heart-breaking* and *blue-eyed*, the second element is an adjective or a participle and the first modifies or completes it. Compound verbs are thinner on the ground and usually formed by conversion or back-formation from nouns: *to babysit*, *to proofread*, *to overdo*.

### Teaching block 62
Neo-classical compounds assemble scientific and technical vocabulary out of classical combining forms: *biography*, *geology*, *telephone*, *photograph*. The forms are bound, but in composition they behave like bases, which is why the pattern keeps turning out new technical terms.

### Teaching block 63
One last group takes its cue from rhythm rather than grammar. *Flip-flop*, *ping-pong* and *tick-tock* pair their halves by sound, and what results is a lexical item with a fixed sense rather than a transparent relation between two parts.

### Teaching block 64
well-known — Compound adjective.

### Teaching block 65
blue-eyed — Compound adjective with a participial head.

### Teaching block 66
to babysit — Compound verb.

### Teaching block 67
biography — Neo-classical compound.

### Teaching block 68
ping-pong — Phonologically motivated compound.

### Teaching block 69
Most English compounds are headed, and the head normally comes last. *Bedroom* is a kind of room, *blackbird* a kind of bird, *well-known* an adjective because *known* is. Remove the head and the category goes with it, which is the quickest test for finding one.

### Teaching block 70
What the head cannot tell you is how the parts relate. *A language teacher* teaches a language, or speaks several; the string alone does not choose. *A coffee table* is not made of coffee. Conventional knowledge and context settle what the grammar leaves open.

### Teaching block 71
Some compounds refuse the pattern altogether. *Pickpocket* denotes a person, not a pocket; *turncoat* denotes a person, not a coat. These are exocentric: the whole is not a kind of its head. Meanings of this sort are learned rather than computed, which is why they tend to fossilise.

### Teaching block 72
bedroom — Endocentric: a kind of room.

### Teaching block 73
blackbird — A kind of bird, not simply a black bird.

### Teaching block 74
pickpocket — Exocentric: a person, not a pocket.

### Teaching block 75
turncoat — Exocentric: a person who changes allegiance.

### Teaching block 76
English derivation runs mostly on affixation. Prefixes normally rework meaning and leave the category alone — *unkind*, *rewrite*, *preview* — while suffixes usually change category as well: *kindness*, *modernise*, *readable*. The tendency is a useful first guess, not a rule.

### Teaching block 77
Class I affixes attach close to the base and often disturb its phonology; Class II affixes sit further out, behave more like independent words, and leave stress where they found it. Hence *electric* beside *electricity*, *photograph* beside *photography*, with the stress migrating in each pair. The division is gradient, but its predictions are testable.

### Teaching block 78
Derivation drags spelling along with it. *Happy* becomes *happiness* with *y* turning to *i*; *able* becomes *ability* with one suffix replacing another. Seen from outside these look like irregularity. Seen by affix class, they are the ordinary behaviour of the forms involved.

### Teaching block 79
un-kind — Prefix changes meaning.

### Teaching block 80
kind-ness — Suffix changes category.

### Teaching block 81
read-able — Adjective-forming suffix.

### Teaching block 82
electric → electricity — Morphophonological alternation with a Class I suffix.

### Teaching block 83
*Electric* ends in a /k/ and *electricity* in an /s/; *photograph* stresses its first syllable and *photography* its second. Neither shift is a slip. Each follows regularly from adding a particular suffix to a particular base.

### Teaching block 84
Class I suffixes characteristically retune the base — its vowels, its consonants, its stress — and Class II suffixes characteristically leave it alone. *-ity* and *-ic* belong with the retuners; *-ness* and *-less* do not. The classification is gradient, but it earns its keep by predicting where alternations fall.

### Teaching block 85
Spelling keeps pace. *Happy* → *happiness* turns *y* into *i*, *hope* → *hopeful* keeps its *e*, *make* → *making* drops one before *-ing*. Whole suffixes can be swapped as well: *able* → *ability*, *curious* → *curiosity*. Once the affix class is known, none of this needs a list of exceptions.

### Teaching block 86
electric → electricity — Final /k/ alternates with /s/.

### Teaching block 87
photograph → photography — Stress shift with a Class I suffix.

### Teaching block 88
happy → happiness — Y changes to i.

### Teaching block 89
able → ability — Affix replacement.

### Teaching block 90
English can make a thing smaller or dearer with a suffix. *-let* gives *booklet*, *-ling* gives *duckling*, *-ette* gives *kitchenette*, *-y* gives *doggy*. Augmentation is less grammaticalised: *mega-*, *super-* and *over-* do that work, often with a borrowed air.

### Teaching block 91
Gender marking is vestigial. *Actor/actress*, *waiter/waitress*, *hero/heroine* are pairs inherited from a system English no longer runs, and they are lexical and stylistic rather than grammatical. Many have been abandoned for neutral forms, and that abandonment is a social decision as much as a linguistic one.

### Teaching block 92
Place and time get their own small inventory of affixes: *fore-*, *pre-*, *post-*, *sub-*, *inter-*, and the suffix *-ward*. *Forecast*, *preview*, *postpone*, *submarine*, *international*, *homeward* each locate something in space or in time, productively but not without limit.

### Teaching block 93
booklet — Diminutive with -let.

### Teaching block 94
duckling — Diminutive with -ling.

### Teaching block 95
actress — Feminine suffix, now often replaced.

### Teaching block 96
preview — Temporal prefix pre-.

### Teaching block 97
English denies with a family of prefixes that overlap without being interchangeable: *un-* in *unhappy*, *in-* in *impossible*, *non-* in *non-negotiable*, *dis-* in *dishonest*, *a-* in *atypical*. Which one attaches where is largely a matter of the lexeme’s history, and the members of the family differ in how freely they recruit new bases.

### Teaching block 98
Not every such prefix denies a property. Reversatives undo an action — *unlock*, *untie*, *devalue*, *disconnect* — and removal prefixes take something away, as in *defrost*, *dethrone*, *unmask*. Opposition prefixes set one thing against another: *anti-war*, *counter-argument*, *pro-choice*.

### Teaching block 99
The categories leak into one another and the base decides the reading. *Dis-* can deny, reverse or oppose; *un-* can negate a quality or undo an act. So one prefix may be fully productive in one use and fossilised in another, and no single gloss will cover both.

### Teaching block 100
unhappy — Negative un-.

### Teaching block 101
non-negotiable — Negative non-.

### Teaching block 102
unlock — Reversative un-.

### Teaching block 103
anti-war — Oppositional anti-.

### Teaching block 104
Names slide into ordinary vocabulary with surprising ease. *Shakespearean*, *Victorian*, *Darwinian*, *Thatcherite*, *Londoner*: the suffix contributes ‘relating to’ or ‘a person associated with’, and the result can drift well beyond the name’s original bearer.

### Teaching block 105
Derivatives from places form a large and untidy family — *American*, *European*, *Asian*, *African* — serving as adjectives or nouns, and their formation resists a single rule. *-an*, *-ian*, *-ese*, *-ish*, *-ic* and a bare zero ending all occur, and which ending a name takes is a fact about that name.

### Teaching block 106
Some derivatives shed the name almost entirely. *A sandwich*, *a boycott*, *a diesel*, *a hoover* began as eponyms and now name ordinary things. Etymology records where they came from; morphology describes what they are now, and the two accounts must not be folded together.

### Teaching block 107
Shakespearean — Adjective from a proper name.

### Teaching block 108
Londoner — Noun from a place name.

### Teaching block 109
European — Adjective or noun from a continent name.

### Teaching block 110
sandwich — Lexicalised common noun from a proper name.

### Teaching block 111
Verbs and adjectives turn into nouns by several routes. *-er*, *-or* and *-ant* typically name a person or an instrument — *driver*, *actor*, *assistant* — while *-tion*, *-ment*, *-ance*, *-ness* and *-ity* name an action, a state or a process: *destruction*, *movement*, *performance*, *happiness*, *ability*.

### Teaching block 112
Some nominalisations stay transparent to their base and some do not. *Happiness* is see-through. *Destruction* is related to *destroy* but has its own shape and its own history. Meaning can drift as well, which is why *a building* usually names a structure rather than the act of building it.

### Teaching block 113
Academic and technical prose leans on nominalisation heavily, and the habit has costs. Packing an action into a noun makes the writing abstract and slows the reader. Choosing between *they decided* and *the decision* is a rhetorical decision as much as a morphological one, and worth making on purpose.

### Teaching block 114
driver — Person nominalisation with -er.

### Teaching block 115
actor — Person nominalisation with -or.

### Teaching block 116
destruction — Action nominalisation with -tion.

### Teaching block 117
happiness — State nominalisation with -ness.

### Teaching block 118
Adjectives come from nouns and verbs through a familiar set of suffixes: *childish*, *hopeful*, *readable*, *economic*, with *-ish*, *-ful*, *-able*, *-ic*, *-ous* and *-al* doing the work. What comes out may be gradable, relational or classificatory, and the difference shows in what the adjective will combine with.

### Teaching block 119
Verbs form the same way from nouns and adjectives: *modernise*, *legalise*, *simplify*, *strengthen*, *computerise*, using *-ise/-ize*, *-ify*, *-en* or no affix at all. The usual sense is ‘make or become’ whatever the base names, though the details vary from suffix to suffix.

### Teaching block 120
Conversion and derivation meet at this point. *To empty* adds nothing to *empty*; *to modernise* adds a suffix. Both produce verbs, yet a question about the productivity of one is not a question about the other.

### Teaching block 121
childish — Adjective from a noun with -ish.

### Teaching block 122
readable — Adjective from a verb with -able.

### Teaching block 123
modernise — Verb from an adjective with -ise.

### Teaching block 124
strengthen — Verb from an adjective with -en.

### Teaching block 125
Cardinals name numbers — *one*, *two*, *three*, *ten*, *hundred*, *thousand* — and they combine recursively into *three hundred and forty-two* or *two thousand five hundred*. The system generates indefinitely and still has to be learned in places.

### Teaching block 126
Ordinals rank (*first*, *second*, *third*, *fourth*), fractions divide (*half*, *quarter*, *third*, *two-fifths*), and dates run numerals together with calendar convention: *the third of May*, *May 3rd*, *twenty twenty-six*.

### Teaching block 127
Numerals also enter compounds. *Two-door*, *three-piece*, *four-wheel-drive*, *ten-year-old* use the numeral as a modifier, and the unit noun stays singular inside: *a ten-year-old child*, never *a ten-years-old child*. The compound has frozen the singular while the meaning stays plural.

### Teaching block 128
three hundred and forty-two — Composite cardinal numeral.

### Teaching block 129
first, second, third — Ordinal numerals.

### Teaching block 130
two-fifths — Fraction.

### Teaching block 131
a ten-year-old child — Numerical compound with singular year.

### Teaching block 132
Vocabulary grows along several routes at once. Borrowing takes a word from another language, semantic change gives an old word a new sense, coinage invents a form outright, and word-formation builds one from pieces already in the language. These routes interact, and a single item may travel more than one of them.

### Teaching block 133
*Policeability* is well formed and unlisted. Whether it becomes established depends on usage — frequency, acceptance, fashion — not on its morphology. A nonce-word may never spread. Dictionaries record what has been established; they do not fix the limits of what is possible.

### Teaching block 134
Productivity itself moves. *-ric* built *bishopric* and then stopped; *-able* and *-ness* are still in service. Borrowed patterns behave the same way, with foreign plurals persisting, fading or settling into a division of labour with native forms.

### Teaching block 135
policeability — Potential word from productive suffixes.

### Teaching block 136
priestric — Not admitted because -ric is no longer productive.

### Teaching block 137
smog — Blend that became established.

### Teaching block 138
sandwich — Lexicalised common noun from a proper name.

### Teaching block 139
English has taken words from Latin, French, Greek, Norse and many other sources, and the borrowed forms do not stay foreign. *Nation* supports *national*, *nationalise* and *nationalisation*, running through productive English patterns like any native base. Borrowing is not itself a morphological process, but it supplies the material that morphology works on.

### Teaching block 140
Classical combining forms carry much of the technical vocabulary: *bio-*, *geo-*, *tele-*, *photo-*, *graph-*, *-ology*, *-graphy*. They pair with one another in *biography* and *geology* and with free bases in *photograph* and *telephone*. Their meanings are usually more specific than those of native affixes, which is why they suit technical coinage.

### Teaching block 141
Borrowed plurals and derivational patterns can be irregular or semi-productive. *Formulae*, *curricula* and *phenomena* keep their foreign plurals while other borrowings have been anglicised, and one and the same item may support both forms with a difference of register or sense.

### Teaching block 142
nation → national → nationalise — Borrowed base in productive derivation.

### Teaching block 143
biography — Neo-classical compound.

### Teaching block 144
geology — Classical combining forms.

### Teaching block 145
formulae / formulas — Foreign and anglicised plurals.

### Teaching block 146
Three questions organise everything in this chapter. Is the form grammatical? Is it established? And if it is both, what internal structure does it have? *Kingdom* is established, *policeability* is grammatical without being established, and a nonce-word is the second kind, used once and dropped. None of those verdicts is about taste.

### Teaching block 147
Complex words are bases and affixes arranged in layers, and the arrangement explains behaviour that a flat list of pieces cannot. Productivity and lexicalisation account for the gap between a pattern that still makes words and a formation surviving only in what it has already made. Around the edges sit manufacture, initialism, clipping, blending, back-formation and phonological modification.

### Teaching block 148
Conversion shifts a word between categories without changing its form. Compounding joins bases into nouns, adjectives and verbs, classical combining forms included. Derivation supplies negation, evaluation, gender, location, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation and the numeral patterns — most of the vocabulary-building machinery English has.

### Teaching block 149
A word-formation checklist: Identify the base and the process: conversion, compounding, derivation, clipping, blending or back-formation. Check whether the pattern is productive and whether the result is established, potential or nonce. Then analyse the constituent structure and the meaning relation between the parts.

### Teaching block 150
Take *The editor’s useful guide was republished after a surprisingly readable rewrite*. *Editor* is an established person nominalisation; *useful* is an adjective formed with *-ful*; *republished* contains the prefix *re-*; *readable* is a potential or established adjective formed with *-able*; *rewrite* is a conversion from verb to noun with the prefix *re-*.

### Teaching block 151
The example shows several word-formation processes at once: derivation, prefixation, conversion and nominalisation. Each form has a base and an affix or a converted category, and each contributes to the meaning of the sentence. The distinction between established and potential words matters for deciding which forms belong to the vocabulary and which are merely possible.

### Teaching block 152
Identify the base and the process. Is the word simple or complex? Is it formed by conversion, compounding, derivation, clipping, blending or back-formation? Then analyse the constituent structure and the meaning relation between the parts.

### Teaching block 153
Decide whether the formation is established, potential or nonce. Check whether the pattern is productive and whether an established synonym blocks it. Do not confuse a stylistic preference with a morphological ungrammaticality.

### Teaching block 154
For derivation, identify the affix class and any morphophonological or spelling alternation. For compounds, identify the head and the relation between the elements. For numerals and proper-name derivatives, check the conventional patterns and any lexicalised meanings.

### Teaching block 155
In *The editor’s useful guide was republished after a surprisingly readable rewrite*, *editor* is a person nominalisation, *useful* is an adjective with *-ful*, *republished* contains *re-*, *readable* contains *-able*, and *rewrite* is a converted noun. The forms illustrate derivation, prefixation, conversion and nominalisation.

### Teaching block 156
Lexical word-formation creates new lexemes. Established, potential and nonce-words differ in vocabulary status, not simply in grammaticality. Complex words have hierarchical base-affix structure, and productivity determines which patterns can create new forms.

### Teaching block 157
Minor processes, conversion and compounding extend the vocabulary alongside derivation. Affixation covers negation, evaluation, gender, location, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation and numerals. Morphological analysis must distinguish form, meaning, productivity and lexical status.

## Outcomes
- o1: Explain the main ideas in Punctuation.
- o2: Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
- o3: Use the ideas when you read and write.

## Key terms
- **punctuation** — The use of marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications to indicate structure and meaning in writing.
- **punctuation indicator** — A punctuation mark, space, or non-segmental modification such as italics or capitals.
- **segmental** — Occupying a position in the linear sequence of writing, as marks and spaces do.
- **non-segmental** — A modification such as italics, bold face or capitalisation that does not occupy a separate position.
- **punctuation mark** — A written symbol such as a comma, full stop or question mark.
- **character** — A graphical shape used to realise one or more punctuation indicators.
- **primary terminal** — A full stop, question mark or exclamation mark marking the end of an orthographic sentence.
- **secondary boundary mark** — A comma, semicolon or colon marking boundaries within or between clauses.
- **delimiting comma** — A comma pair enclosing a supplement or parenthetical element.
- **parenthesis** — A pair of round or square brackets enclosing material.
- **dash** — A punctuation indicator used for interruption, supplement or range.
- **quotation mark** — A paired indicator enclosing quoted or highlighted material.
- **capitalisation** — The use of upper-case letters for sentence beginnings, proper names or emphasis.
- **orthographic sentence** — A unit of writing beginning with a capital and ending with a primary terminal.
- **orthographic word** — A minimal unit of writing flanked by spaces or punctuation.
- **hyphen** — A word-internal mark joining parts of a compound or a line break.
- **long hyphen** — A mark used in some styles to join coordinated names or relationships.
- **apostrophe** — A word-internal mark used for omission or the genitive.
- **ellipsis points** — Three dots marking omission or a trailing off.
- **abbreviation full stop** — A full stop marking an abbreviation, as in Col. Blimp.
- **slash** — A mark used for alternatives, fractions, dates or line breaks.
- **light punctuation** — A style using relatively few optional marks, especially commas.
- **heavy punctuation** — A style using more optional marks, especially commas.
- **asyndetic** — Coordination without an overt coordinator.
- **supplement** — A detached element set off from the clause, often by commas, dashes or parentheses.
- **vocative** — An expression naming the person addressed, often set off by commas.
- **connective adjunct** — An expression such as however that links a clause to surrounding discourse.

## Chapter article
### Section: The domain of punctuation
A page of English is held together by things that occupy positions in the line: full stops, commas, semicolons, colons, question marks, quotation marks, brackets. These are segmental, and so are the spaces between words — which is why spaces count as punctuation. They separate, and separating is the job.

Other indicators take up no position at all. Italics, bold face, small capitals and capitalisation modify the default roman lower case in place. Italics can carry a title or a quotation; a capital can announce a sentence. Because nothing is inserted into the line, it is easy to forget that these are punctuation too.

The domain has edges, and they are not sharp. The apostrophe and the ordinary hyphen work inside words. Accents belong to spelling rather than punctuation, though the diaeresis in *coöperate* sits awkwardly between the two. Quotation marks and brackets can enclose several sentences, and a paragraph break can mark a boundary; the layout of chapters and headings does not.

#### Punctuation indicators
| Type | Examples | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Segmental mark | . , ; : ? ! | Occupies a position |
| Segmental space | word space | Separates words |
| Non-segmental modification | italics, bold, capitals | Modifies default form |
| Word-internal mark | apostrophe, hyphen | Within a word |
| Beyond the sentence | quotation marks, parentheses | Can enclose multiple sentences |

#### Quick check
- prompt: Why are spaces part of punctuation?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: They are segmental units that separate words in writing.
      feedback: They occupy positions in the linear sequence.
    - id: b
      text: They are non-segmental.
      feedback: Spaces are segmental.
    - id: c
      text: They mark sentence boundaries only.
      feedback: They mark word boundaries too.
  - answer: a

### Section: Indicators and characters
Compare the mark in *Kim’s report* with the mark in *the word ‘bank’*. They may look identical, and in many fonts they are. Functionally they are different indicators — an apostrophe and a single quotation mark — and naming them by shape alone conceals that. An indicator is a job; a character is a shape that may do more than one job.

Pairs complicate the picture. Quotation marks open and close, and a font with distinct opening and closing characters makes the pairing visible, while a font without them uses one shape for both positions. The dash, the ordinary hyphen and the long hyphen are three further indicators, realised by different characters and different spacing.

The full stop is the clearest case of one character serving several functions: it ends a sentence, marks an abbreviation, and appears three at a time in ellipsis points. Only the first two share a realisation. Ellipsis points are a separate indicator that happens to be built from the same character.

#### Indicators and characters
| Indicator | Character(s) | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Apostrophe | ’ or ' | Omission or genitive |
| Single quotation mark | ‘ ’ or ' | Quotation |
| Dash | —, –, - or -- | Interruption or range |
| Ordinary hyphen | - | Word-internal joining |
| Ellipsis points | ... | Omission or trailing off |
| Full stop | . | Sentence terminal or abbreviation |

#### Quick check
- prompt: Why are apostrophe and single quotation mark distinct indicators?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: They have different functions even when realised by the same character.
      feedback: The apostrophe cannot be realised by the opening quotation character.
    - id: b
      text: They always use different characters.
      feedback: They can share a character.
    - id: c
      text: They are both non-segmental.
      feedback: Both are segmental marks.
  - answer: a

### Section: The status of punctuation rules
Style manuals codify punctuation, which makes it look like law. It is not law. Some marks the orthographic system demands; others are conventions a publisher can adopt or drop. Punctuation shows less social variation than grammar, but it varies by region, by period and by house style, and those variations are not errors.

The most visible axis is weight. Light punctuation uses few optional commas, heavy punctuation many. *On Sundays they like to have a picnic lunch in the park if it’s fine* is the light version; *On Sundays, they like to have a picnic lunch in the park, if it’s fine* is the heavy one. Neither is a mistake, and a careful writer keeps to one convention within a document.

Quotation conventions divide along the same lines. American practice tends to put commas and full stops inside the closing quotation mark; British practice often puts them where the logic of the sentence puts them. The disagreement is about convention, not grammar, and consistency matters more than the choice.

#### Light and heavy punctuation
- example: On Sundays they like to have a picnic lunch in the park if it’s fine. — Light punctuation: few optional commas.
- example: On Sundays, they like to have a picnic lunch in the park, if it’s fine. — Heavy punctuation: more optional commas.
- example: He said, ‘I’m leaving.’ — Quotation with comma before the quote.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What is the difference between light and heavy punctuation?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: Light uses fewer optional marks; heavy uses more.
      feedback: The difference concerns optional commas and similar marks.
    - id: b
      text: Light is grammatical; heavy is ungrammatical.
      feedback: Both are conventional styles.
    - id: c
      text: Heavy uses no full stops.
      feedback: Full stops are required in both.
  - answer: a

### Section: Orthographic sentences and words
What makes a sentence a sentence on the page? A capital at the front and a terminal at the back. The definition is circular in a useful way: the orthographic sentence is a unit of writing, and it need not match a syntactic sentence. Two main clauses can form one orthographic sentence or two, and the punctuation decides which.

Orthographic words work the same way. A word, for the purposes of writing, is whatever sits between spaces or punctuation. *Greenhouse* is one such unit and one compound; *green house* is two units and a syntactic construction. The definition tracks typography, not grammar.

None of this licenses reading punctuation as prosody. Speech has intonation and pause; writing has its own inventory. A comma may fall where a speaker would pause, or where a grammatical boundary lies, or simply where a style wants a mark. Any account that reduces it to one of these fails on the other two.

#### Orthographic and grammatical units
- example: You will have to make a decision soon. It is not for me to influence you. — Two orthographic sentences.
- example: By all means take the report with you, but be sure to return it. — One orthographic sentence with two coordinated clauses.
- example: greenhouse / green house — One compound word versus two words.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What defines an orthographic sentence?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: A capital letter at the beginning and a primary terminal at the end
      feedback: This is a unit of writing, not necessarily a syntactic sentence.
    - id: b
      text: A clause with a subject and predicate
      feedback: That is a syntactic definition.
    - id: c
      text: A paragraph
      feedback: A paragraph can contain several sentences.
  - answer: a

### Section: Functions of punctuation
Punctuation marks boundaries at every scale. Spaces divide words, terminals divide sentences, and commas with their relatives divide smaller stretches inside the sentence. Boundary marking turns up almost everywhere, which is why it is usually treated as the primary function.

Marks also carry status. A question mark makes a question, an exclamation mark an exclamation, quotation marks a quotation or a highlighted word. Capitals flag sentence openings and proper names. These tell a reader how to take the unit, not merely where it stops.

Then there is grouping, and there is omission. Brackets and dashes set supplementary material apart; commas can do the same; colons and semicolons signal a relation between clauses. Apostrophes, ellipsis points and abbreviation stops mark material that has been dropped or reduced. A single mark can serve more than one of these ends.

#### Functions of punctuation
| Function | Examples | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary | . , ; : ? ! | Marks units and sub-units |
| Status | ? ! quotation marks | Signals question, exclamation or quotation |
| Grouping | parentheses, dashes, commas | Sets off supplements and parentheticals |
| Omission | apostrophe, ellipsis | Marks missing material |
| Abbreviation | Col. | Marks a reduced word |

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which function is primary in punctuation?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: Marking boundaries
      feedback: Boundary marking is involved in virtually all punctuation.
    - id: b
      text: Marking emphasis
      feedback: Emphasis is one use, not the primary function.
    - id: c
      text: Marking pronunciation
      feedback: Punctuation is not a direct transcription of speech.
  - answer: a

### Section: Primary terminals
Three marks end an orthographic sentence: the full stop, the question mark and the exclamation mark. These are the primary terminals, and choosing among them is choosing a status — statement, question, exclamation — with the full stop as the unmarked default.

Informal writing sometimes piles marks together for emphasis. That is a stylistic gesture rather than a grammatical one, and it is rare in academic or legal prose.

The full stop has a second life inside abbreviations: *Col. Blimp*. The character is the same as the sentence terminal, the function is not. Ellipsis points, though made of the same dots, are a separate indicator for omission or a trailing off.

#### Primary terminals
- example: The meeting is over. — Full stop marks a statement.
- example: Is the meeting over? — Question mark marks a question.
- example: The meeting is over! — Exclamation mark marks an exclamation.
- example: Col. Blimp — Full stop marks an abbreviation.

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which mark is a primary terminal?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: A question mark
      feedback: It marks the end of an orthographic sentence.
    - id: b
      text: A comma
      feedback: A comma is a secondary boundary mark.
    - id: c
      text: A hyphen
      feedback: A hyphen is word-internal.
  - answer: a

### Section: Comma, semicolon, and colon
Inside the sentence, three marks carry the boundary work. The comma is the flexible member of the set; the semicolon and the colon are specialists. All three mark boundaries, though boundaries of different weight and different kinds.

The semicolon joins main clauses that are closely related but not linked by a conjunction: *The road was closed; we had to take a detour*. The colon points forward, introducing an explanation, a list or a quotation: *The reason was simple: nobody had checked the figures*.

The comma covers the most ground — coordination, supplementation, asyndetic sequences, vocatives, some boundaries below the clause. Whether a given comma is obligatory, optional or merely stylistic depends on the construction and on the style in force. It is not a pause written down.

#### Secondary boundaries
- example: The road was closed; we had to take a detour. — Semicolon between related main clauses.
- example: The reason was simple: nobody had checked the figures. — Colon introduces an explanation.
- example: Jo, close the door. — Comma sets off a vocative.

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which mark typically separates closely related main clauses without a conjunction?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: A semicolon
      feedback: The road was closed; we had to take a detour.
    - id: b
      text: A question mark
      feedback: That is a primary terminal.
    - id: c
      text: An apostrophe
      feedback: That is word-internal.
  - answer: a

### Section: Comma uses and delimiting commas
Consider two commas in very different jobs. In *Kim went to the concert, but Pat stayed at home* the comma marks the join between coordinated clauses; in *Some went by bus, some by train* it marks a sequence with no coordinator at all. Same mark, different boundary.

Delimiting commas come in pairs and enclose. *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* puts a supplement between two marks, and a single comma would leave the reader unsure where the aside ends. The pair is the unit, not either comma on its own.

That pairing does grammatical work. *The students who passed were congratulated* restricts the reference to those who passed. *The students, who passed, were congratulated* treats the passing as extra information about all of them. The commas do not decorate a difference in meaning; they signal a difference in structure.

#### Comma functions
- example: Kim went to the concert, but Pat stayed at home. — Comma between coordinated clauses.
- example: My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida. — Delimiting commas around a supplement.
- example: The students who passed were congratulated. — No commas: integrated relative.
- example: The students, who passed, were congratulated. — Delimiting commas: supplementary relative.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What do the commas do in My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: They delimit a supplementary relative clause.
      feedback: The relative adds information rather than restricting the antecedent.
    - id: b
      text: They mark a coordination.
      feedback: There is no coordination.
    - id: c
      text: They mark an abbreviation.
      feedback: No abbreviation is involved.
  - answer: a

### Section: Parentheses and the dash
Brackets hold material aside. What they enclose can be a word, a phrase, a clause or several sentences, and the closing bracket mirrors the opening one. The effect is a whisper: present in the sentence, but subordinate to its main line.

The dash is louder. It can introduce a supplement, cut a thought short or set off an apposition: *The editor—usually meticulous—left the paragraph unmarked*. Informal and literary prose uses dashes freely; formal prose is more sparing.

Put the same aside in brackets and in dashes and the difference is emphasis. Brackets push the material into the background; dashes pull it forward or register an interruption. Grammar permits either, and rhetoric does not make them interchangeable.

#### Parentheses and dashes
- example: The editor (usually meticulous) left the paragraph unmarked. — Parentheses background the supplement.
- example: The editor—usually meticulous—left the paragraph unmarked. — Dashes foreground or interrupt.
- example: There were three options—tea, coffee, or water. — Dash introduces a list.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What is the difference between parentheses and dashes in supplements?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: Parentheses tend to background; dashes tend to foreground or interrupt.
      feedback: The effect is stylistic and rhetorical.
    - id: b
      text: Parentheses are grammatical; dashes are ungrammatical.
      feedback: Both are grammatical.
    - id: c
      text: Dashes mark abbreviations.
      feedback: That is a different function.
  - answer: a

### Section: Quotation marks and related indicators
Quotation marks fence off material that is being cited, named or held at arm’s length: direct speech, titles, words used as words. Single and double marks are distinct indicators even when a font realises them with one character, and they normally come in pairs.

How quotation marks interact with neighbouring punctuation is a matter of regional and house convention. American style tends to place commas and full stops inside the closing mark; British style often follows the syntax. Each is regular within its own system, and mixing them inside one document is what creates trouble.

The marks also do lighter work: scare quotes that signal scepticism, metalinguistic quotation that names a word rather than using it, and titles of short works. Italics overlap with several of these functions, especially for titles. Choosing between the two is a convention, not a grammatical requirement.

#### Quotation conventions
- example: She said, ‘I’m leaving.’ — Single quotation marks enclose direct speech.
- example: She said, “I’m leaving.” — Double quotation marks in another style.
- example: The word ‘bank’ has several meanings. — Quotation marks mark a word used as a word.
- example: His ‘apology’ was not convincing. — Scare quotes signal scepticism.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What do quotation marks do in The word ‘bank’ has several meanings?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: They mark a word used as a word.
      feedback: This is a metalinguistic use.
    - id: b
      text: They mark a question.
      feedback: A question mark does that.
    - id: c
      text: They mark an abbreviation.
      feedback: No abbreviation is involved.
  - answer: a

### Section: Capitalisation
A capital is punctuation that leaves no mark in the line: it changes a letter’s shape instead of inserting something. It marks the start of an orthographic sentence, the conventional form of a proper name, and — depending on style — the words of a title.

The sentence-initial capital is part of what defines the orthographic sentence; without it the unit is incomplete. Proper names have conventions of their own, some lexical and some grammatical. Titles vary widely, with some styles capitalising every major word and others only the first word and the names.

It is a mistake to read every capital as emphasis. Most mark structure — a sentence opening, a name, a heading — and emphatic capitals belong to informal registers. One letter shape does several jobs, and context decides which.

#### Capitalisation uses
- example: The meeting is over. — Sentence-initial capital.
- example: We met Kim in London. — Proper-name capitals.
- example: The Lord of the Rings — Title capitalisation in one style.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What does the initial capital in The meeting is over mark?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: The beginning of an orthographic sentence
      feedback: Sentence-initial capitals are part of the orthographic sentence definition.
    - id: b
      text: A proper name
      feedback: The is not a proper name here.
    - id: c
      text: An abbreviation
      feedback: No abbreviation is involved.
  - answer: a

### Section: Word-level punctuation: spaces and hyphens
The space is punctuation’s least visible indicator and one of its most consequential. *Greenhouse* is one word on the page; *green house* is two. The difference is typographic, and a grammatical difference travels with it.

The ordinary hyphen joins the parts of a compound or breaks a word across lines: *non-negotiable*, *well-known*. The long hyphen links coordinated names and relationships: *the doctor–patient relationship*. The dash, which looks similar at small sizes, is a different indicator doing a different job.

Hyphenation is part convention and part grammar. Compound nouns may be written open, hyphenated or solid, and the choice tracks style and the compound’s degree of lexicalisation. Hyphens also disambiguate, as *a small-business owner* against *a small business owner* shows.

#### Spaces and hyphens
- example: greenhouse / green house — One compound word versus two words.
- example: non-negotiable — Ordinary hyphen in a compound.
- example: the doctor–patient relationship — Long hyphen joining coordinated names.
- example: a small-business owner — Hyphen disambiguates the compound.

#### Quick check
- prompt: What does the hyphen do in a small-business owner?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: It marks small-business as a compound modifier.
      feedback: It disambiguates from a small business owner.
    - id: b
      text: It marks a sentence boundary.
      feedback: A hyphen is word-internal.
    - id: c
      text: It marks an abbreviation.
      feedback: No abbreviation is involved.
  - answer: a

### Section: Apostrophe, abbreviation stop, and slash
The apostrophe works inside words. It marks omission in *don’t* and *rock ’n’ roll*, and the genitive in *Kim’s* and *dogs’*. It is not the single quotation mark, even where one character serves both, and its position follows the morphology and spelling of the word.

The abbreviation stop marks a reduced word: *Col. Blimp*, *e.g.*, *i.e.* Practice varies by style and region, and many styles drop the stops in acronyms and initialisms. This is a use of the full stop, not a separate mark.

The slash is a general-purpose separator: alternatives in *and/or*, fractions in *3/4*, dates in *9/11*, line breaks in quoted verse. It is conventional, occasionally ambiguous, and — like the rest of the system — a fact about writing rather than about speech.

#### Apostrophe, abbreviation, slash
- example: don’t — Apostrophe marks omission.
- example: Kim’s report — Apostrophe marks the genitive.
- example: Col. Blimp — Full stop marks an abbreviation.
- example: and/or — Slash marks alternatives.

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which use of the apostrophe is word-internal?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: The apostrophe in don’t
      feedback: It marks omission inside a word.
    - id: b
      text: The full stop in Col.
      feedback: That is an abbreviation stop.
    - id: c
      text: The slash in and/or
      feedback: That is a slash.
  - answer: a

### Section: Chapter Review
Segmental marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications: punctuation is a writing system built from those. The distinction to keep is between the indicator, which is a function, and the character, which is a shape. The apostrophe and the single quotation mark show why it matters: different jobs, sometimes one shape.

Rules sit at three levels. Some marks the orthographic system requires, some are conventions of region and house, and some are choices of weight and tone. The orthographic sentence and the orthographic word are defined by these marks rather than by syntax, which is why the two descriptions can diverge.

Terminals close sentences; secondary marks divide what lies inside them. Brackets and dashes handle supplements, quotation marks and capitals handle status, hyphens and apostrophes handle the insides of words. That the system is conventional does not make it arbitrary. The conventions are learnable, and they are learned.

#### A punctuation checklist
Identify the indicator and its function. Decide whether it marks a boundary, status, grouping, omission or abbreviation. Check whether the mark is required, optional or stylistic. Then consider the house style, region and light or heavy punctuation convention.

#### Quick check
- prompt: Which statement correctly describes punctuation?
  - options:
    - id: a
      text: It is a writing system using marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications.
      feedback: It is not a direct transcription of speech.
    - id: b
      text: It is exactly the same as prosody.
      feedback: Punctuation and prosody are related but distinct.
    - id: c
      text: It has no optional conventions.
      feedback: Light and heavy styles show optional variation.
  - answer: a

## Teaching blocks
### Teaching block 1
Read a page aloud and you will hear pauses the page does not contain, and see marks that speech has no equivalent for. Punctuation is a system of its own: marks, spaces and modifications such as italics and capitals, arranged to show where units begin and end, what status a stretch of writing carries, and what has been left out. It is not a transcription of speech, and treating it as one produces most of the confusion the subject attracts.

### Teaching block 2
The chapter first fixes the domain — what counts as punctuation and what falls outside it — and separates the functional indicator from the graphical character that realises it. From there it asks how binding the rules are, how orthographic sentences and words differ from syntactic ones, and what punctuation actually does. The remaining sections take the marks family by family: terminals and boundary marks, brackets and dashes, quotation, capitals, hyphens, apostrophes, stops and slashes.

### Teaching block 3
One theme recurs. Some marks the writing system requires, some are conventions that vary by region and house style, and some are choices of tone. Any description that flattens those levels will mistake a preference for a rule.

### Teaching block 4
A page of English is held together by things that occupy positions in the line: full stops, commas, semicolons, colons, question marks, quotation marks, brackets. These are segmental, and so are the spaces between words — which is why spaces count as punctuation. They separate, and separating is the job.

### Teaching block 5
Other indicators take up no position at all. Italics, bold face, small capitals and capitalisation modify the default roman lower case in place. Italics can carry a title or a quotation; a capital can announce a sentence. Because nothing is inserted into the line, it is easy to forget that these are punctuation too.

### Teaching block 6
The domain has edges, and they are not sharp. The apostrophe and the ordinary hyphen work inside words. Accents belong to spelling rather than punctuation, though the diaeresis in *coöperate* sits awkwardly between the two. Quotation marks and brackets can enclose several sentences, and a paragraph break can mark a boundary; the layout of chapters and headings does not.

### Teaching block 7
Punctuation indicators

### Teaching block 8
Segmental mark | . , ; : ? ! | Occupies a position

### Teaching block 9
Segmental space | word space | Separates words

### Teaching block 10
Non-segmental modification | italics, bold, capitals | Modifies default form

### Teaching block 11
Word-internal mark | apostrophe, hyphen | Within a word

### Teaching block 12
Beyond the sentence | quotation marks, parentheses | Can enclose multiple sentences

### Teaching block 13
Compare the mark in *Kim’s report* with the mark in *the word ‘bank’*. They may look identical, and in many fonts they are. Functionally they are different indicators — an apostrophe and a single quotation mark — and naming them by shape alone conceals that. An indicator is a job; a character is a shape that may do more than one job.

### Teaching block 14
Pairs complicate the picture. Quotation marks open and close, and a font with distinct opening and closing characters makes the pairing visible, while a font without them uses one shape for both positions. The dash, the ordinary hyphen and the long hyphen are three further indicators, realised by different characters and different spacing.

### Teaching block 15
The full stop is the clearest case of one character serving several functions: it ends a sentence, marks an abbreviation, and appears three at a time in ellipsis points. Only the first two share a realisation. Ellipsis points are a separate indicator that happens to be built from the same character.

### Teaching block 16
Indicators and characters

### Teaching block 17
Apostrophe | ’ or ' | Omission or genitive

### Teaching block 18
Single quotation mark | ‘ ’ or ' | Quotation

### Teaching block 19
Dash | —, –, - or -- | Interruption or range

### Teaching block 20
Ordinary hyphen | - | Word-internal joining

### Teaching block 21
Ellipsis points | ... | Omission or trailing off

### Teaching block 22
Full stop | . | Sentence terminal or abbreviation

### Teaching block 23
Style manuals codify punctuation, which makes it look like law. It is not law. Some marks the orthographic system demands; others are conventions a publisher can adopt or drop. Punctuation shows less social variation than grammar, but it varies by region, by period and by house style, and those variations are not errors.

### Teaching block 24
The most visible axis is weight. Light punctuation uses few optional commas, heavy punctuation many. *On Sundays they like to have a picnic lunch in the park if it’s fine* is the light version; *On Sundays, they like to have a picnic lunch in the park, if it’s fine* is the heavy one. Neither is a mistake, and a careful writer keeps to one convention within a document.

### Teaching block 25
Quotation conventions divide along the same lines. American practice tends to put commas and full stops inside the closing quotation mark; British practice often puts them where the logic of the sentence puts them. The disagreement is about convention, not grammar, and consistency matters more than the choice.

### Teaching block 26
On Sundays they like to have a picnic lunch in the park if it’s fine. — Light punctuation: few optional commas.

### Teaching block 27
On Sundays, they like to have a picnic lunch in the park, if it’s fine. — Heavy punctuation: more optional commas.

### Teaching block 28
He said, ‘I’m leaving.’ — Quotation with comma before the quote.

### Teaching block 29
What makes a sentence a sentence on the page? A capital at the front and a terminal at the back. The definition is circular in a useful way: the orthographic sentence is a unit of writing, and it need not match a syntactic sentence. Two main clauses can form one orthographic sentence or two, and the punctuation decides which.

### Teaching block 30
Orthographic words work the same way. A word, for the purposes of writing, is whatever sits between spaces or punctuation. *Greenhouse* is one such unit and one compound; *green house* is two units and a syntactic construction. The definition tracks typography, not grammar.

### Teaching block 31
None of this licenses reading punctuation as prosody. Speech has intonation and pause; writing has its own inventory. A comma may fall where a speaker would pause, or where a grammatical boundary lies, or simply where a style wants a mark. Any account that reduces it to one of these fails on the other two.

### Teaching block 32
You will have to make a decision soon. It is not for me to influence you. — Two orthographic sentences.

### Teaching block 33
By all means take the report with you, but be sure to return it. — One orthographic sentence with two coordinated clauses.

### Teaching block 34
greenhouse / green house — One compound word versus two words.

### Teaching block 35
Punctuation marks boundaries at every scale. Spaces divide words, terminals divide sentences, and commas with their relatives divide smaller stretches inside the sentence. Boundary marking turns up almost everywhere, which is why it is usually treated as the primary function.

### Teaching block 36
Marks also carry status. A question mark makes a question, an exclamation mark an exclamation, quotation marks a quotation or a highlighted word. Capitals flag sentence openings and proper names. These tell a reader how to take the unit, not merely where it stops.

### Teaching block 37
Then there is grouping, and there is omission. Brackets and dashes set supplementary material apart; commas can do the same; colons and semicolons signal a relation between clauses. Apostrophes, ellipsis points and abbreviation stops mark material that has been dropped or reduced. A single mark can serve more than one of these ends.

### Teaching block 101
Take *The editor—usually meticulous—left the final paragraph unmarked; the typesetter, however, noticed it immediately*. The dashes delimit the supplement *usually meticulous*. The semicolon separates two closely related main clauses. The comma after *typesetter* sets off the connective adjunct *however*.

### Teaching block 102
The example shows boundary, grouping and status functions at once. The dashes mark a supplement; the semicolon marks a clause boundary; the comma marks a supplement-like connective. None of these marks is a direct transcription of a pause, and each has a conventional function in the written sentence.

### Teaching block 103
Identify the punctuation indicator and its function. Is it a primary terminal, a secondary boundary mark, a parenthesis, a dash, a quotation mark, a capital, a hyphen, an apostrophe or a slash? Then decide whether it marks a boundary, status, grouping, omission or abbreviation.

### Teaching block 104
Check whether the mark is required, optional or stylistic. Light and heavy styles differ in optional commas; regional and house styles differ in quotation conventions. Do not treat a stylistic preference as a grammatical rule.

### Teaching block 105
Distinguish the orthographic sentence and word from syntactic units. Punctuation defines units of writing, not necessarily units of grammar. The same sequence can be one sentence or two, one word or two, depending on the punctuation.

### Teaching block 106
In *The editor—usually meticulous—left the final paragraph unmarked; the typesetter, however, noticed it immediately*, the dashes delimit a supplement, the semicolon separates two main clauses, and the comma sets off the connective adjunct *however*. The marks indicate boundaries and grouping, not pronunciation.

### Teaching block 107
Punctuation uses segmental marks, spaces and non-segmental modifications to organise writing. Indicators are functional categories; characters are their graphical realisations. Primary terminals mark sentence boundaries; secondary marks mark smaller boundaries and relations.

### Teaching block 108
Parentheses and dashes set off supplements; quotation marks and capitals mark status; hyphens and apostrophes operate within words. Punctuation rules vary by style, region and house convention, and they are not a direct representation of prosody.
